usage: the standard 요-form to an adult you respect
반말, only to a close friend, junior, or child
hang in there a bit more
조금만 softens it to almost there
examples: 힘내! 너는 할 수 있어.
Cheer up! You can do it.
반말 to a close friend; pairs naturally with 할 수 있어
많이 힘들죠? 힘내세요.
It's hard, isn't it? Stay strong.
everyday comfort to a coworker; 힘들죠 invites them to agree
수술 잘 끝났대요. 아버님, 힘내세요.
They say the surgery went well. Stay strong, sir.
real situation — encouraging a worried family member, raised with 아버님
nuance: 힘내세요 is built from 힘 (strength) + 내다 (to put out/summon), so literally it is 'summon your strength' — you are urging someone to gather energy and push through a hard patch, not merely feeling sorry for them. Compare it with 괜찮아요 (it's okay), which only soothes; 힘내세요 actively pushes the person forward, so it fits before or during a struggle (an exam, illness, job loss), whereas pure sympathy like 안타깝네요 fits after a loss when there is nothing left to push toward. It collocates with 조금만 (just a little) and 같이 (together). Register matters: drop to 힘내 only with friends or juniors — saying 힘내 to your boss sounds presumptuous, so keep -세요. The English-speaker pitfall is reaching for 'cheer up' and expecting the same lightness; 힘내세요 carries real emotional weight and can feel too strong if someone is only mildly down, where a simple 파이팅! is lighter and more casual.

mistakes: Saying 힘내 to a senior or boss
힘내 is 반말 and sounds like an order to an equal or junior; to anyone you respect it feels disrespectful. Use 힘내세요 instead.
Using 힘내세요 for mild, passing disappointment
It implies a genuine ordeal worth mustering strength for; for a small letdown it overdramatizes. A casual 파이팅! or 괜찮아요 fits better there.
Translating 'cheer up' as 기뻐하세요
기뻐하세요 commands someone to literally feel joy, which is unnatural and pushy. The set phrase for encouragement is 힘내세요.

usage: 반말 to a friend, junior, or child
참 has a warm, slightly childlike ring — classic to kids
examples: 우와, 잘했어!
Wow, good job!
반말 reacting to a friend's small win
발표 잘했어요. 준비 많이 했네요.
You presented well. You prepared a lot.
everyday praise after a meeting; 네요 marks fresh realization
혼자 이걸 다 해냈어요? 정말 잘했어요.
You finished all this alone? You really did well.
real situation — praising independence with genuine surprise
nuance: 잘했어요 is 잘 (well) + 했어요 (the past of 하다, to do), so the past tense is the whole point: you praise something already finished, judging the result. Contrast it with 잘하네요, present tense, which admires an ongoing skill ('you're good at this') as you watch, and with 잘될 거예요 ('it'll go well'), which encourages before the fact — using 잘했어요 before someone starts is a logic error. Because 하다 is the most regular verb, the form is simply 하다 → 했어요; there is no irregularity to fear here. Watch the status angle: to a clear superior, bare 잘했어요 can sound like you are grading them from above, so toward a boss Koreans soften to 수고하셨어요 or 잘 보고 들었습니다 rather than praising their performance directly. The English-speaker pitfall is using 'good job' freely upward the way English does; in Korean, praise flows comfortably downward (to juniors, kids, peers) but feels presumptuous aimed up the ladder.

mistakes: Saying 잘했어요 before a task is finished
The past tense judges a completed result; said beforehand it's illogical. Encourage with 잘할 거예요 or 화이팅 instead.
Praising your boss with 잘했어요
Evaluating a superior's work sounds like you outrank them. Toward a senior, use 수고하셨습니다 or express thanks rather than a grade.
Confusing 잘했어요 with 잘하셨어요 for elders
To a respected adult, drop in the honorific -시-: 잘하셨어요. Plain 잘했어요 to an elder can feel a touch flat or familiar.

english: Good work. / Thanks for your effort.
usage: to a peer or junior after shared effort
thank you for your hard work
많다 adds 'a lot of' effort, extra warmth
to someone still working as you leave
examples: 수고했어, 오늘 고마웠어.
Good work, thanks for today.
반말 to a close colleague after a long shift
다들 수고하셨어요. 들어가서 쉬세요.
Everyone worked hard. Go home and rest.
everyday — a team lead wrapping up the day, honorific -시-
이사 도와줘서 정말 수고하셨어요.
Thank you so much for helping me move.
real situation — thanking someone after genuinely tiring help
nuance: 수고 is Sino-Korean 受苦 ('receive-suffering'), so 수고했어요 literally acknowledges that someone has taken on trouble and toil on your or the group's behalf — it thanks the effort itself, not the outcome. That separates it from 잘했어요, which judges how good the result was: a project can flop yet still earn a heartfelt 수고했어요 for the work poured in. It collocates with 많이/많았어요 (a lot) and 오늘도 (today again). The big register trap: many guides say 'never say 수고하셨어요 to a boss,' but in modern workplaces the honorific 수고하셨습니다/수고하셨어요 is widely accepted to seniors; what truly grates is bare 수고했어요 (반말-flavored) aimed upward, or worse 수고하세요 to a superior, which can read as 'keep slaving away.' The English-speaker pitfall is hunting for a single 'thanks for your hard work' and using the casual form everywhere — pick the level by who hears it, and lean on 수고하셨습니다 when in doubt about rank.

Without -시- it carries a peer-to-junior tone that feels too familiar upward. Use 수고하셨습니다 or 수고하셨어요 for seniors.
Telling your boss 수고하세요 as you leave first
To a superior it can sound like 'you keep working away,' faintly cheeky. Better: 먼저 들어가 보겠습니다 / 먼저 가 보겠습니다.
Using 수고했어요 to praise the quality of a result
It thanks effort, not achievement; for a good result say 잘했어요 (down) or 고생하셨습니다. Mixing the two blurs your meaning.

usage: general warning about a hazard, polite
to someone heading out — a caring goodbye
noun + 조심: the thing to beware of comes first
fixed compound — careful with your words
examples: 뜨거우니까 조심해.
It's hot, so be careful.
반말 handing hot food to a friend; -니까 gives the reason
길이 미끄러워요. 발 조심하세요.
The road is slippery. Watch your step.
everyday warning on an icy day; object 발 marks what to guard
밤늦었는데 조심히 들어가세요.
It's late at night, so get home safe.
real situation — seeing a guest off; 조심히 + 가세요/들어가세요 is the warm send-off
nuance: 조심 is Sino-Korean 操心 ('handle/manage the heart'), i.e. to keep your mind alert, so 조심하세요 tells someone to stay watchful and avoid harm. Distinguish two uses: as a literal warning it pairs with the danger named first — 발 조심 (watch your step), 감기 조심 (mind the cold), 차 조심 (watch for cars); but it also works as a caring farewell, where 조심히 가세요/들어가세요 is closer to English 'take care, get home safe' than a real alarm. Note 조심히 (adverb, 'carefully') modifies the verb of going, while 조심하세요 is the standalone command. The English-speaker pitfall is twofold: first, forgetting to front the object, so 'be careful of colds' becomes vague — Koreans say 감기 조심하세요, not just 조심하세요; second, over-warning, since a brisk English 'be careful!' is light, but a bare 조심하세요 with no object can sound abrupt unless you add what to watch for or pair it with 가세요 as a goodbye.

mistakes: Dropping the object when there is a specific hazard
Bare 조심하세요 leaves the danger unnamed and sounds vague. Front it: 발 조심하세요, 감기 조심하세요, 차 조심하세요.
Saying 조심하다 with the wrong particle, e.g. 감기를 조심
Colloquially the noun attaches directly (감기 조심하세요); over-marking with 을/를 sounds stiff. Keep noun + 조심하세요.
Using 조심히 as if it meant 'be careful' on its own
조심히 is an adverb that needs a verb (조심히 가세요). The standalone command is 조심하세요.

usage: warm and polite, before a challenge
-ㅂ니다 for written notes or formal speech
examples: 내일 시험이지? 행운을 빌어!
Your exam's tomorrow, right? Good luck!
반말 cheering on a friend
면접 잘 보세요. 행운을 빌어요.
Do well in the interview. I wish you luck.
everyday encouragement before a one-off event
새 가게 잘되길 바라요. 진심으로 행운을 빕니다.
I hope your new shop thrives. I sincerely wish you luck.
real situation — a formal, heartfelt send-off with 진심으로
nuance: 행운 is Sino-Korean 幸運 ('fortunate luck'), and 빌다 means to pray or beg, so 행운을 빌어요 is literally 'I pray for your good fortune' — a sincere hope that chance favors someone facing an exam, interview, audition, or contest. Note the object particle 을 (행운을), which English speakers often drop. Contrast it with 화이팅!/파이팅! (Fighting!), the breezy cheer Koreans actually shout most of the time: 화이팅 hypes up effort and spirit, while 행운을 빌어요 is gentler and points to luck and outcome, so it sounds warmer and a bit more formal. Beware: 빌다 also means 'to borrow' in other contexts (돈을 빌리다), but here the root is the prayer-빌다 — they are different verbs, so don't second-guess the meaning. The English-speaker pitfall is timing and weight: 'good luck' in English can even be sarcastic, but 행운을 빌어요 is unfailingly sincere and belongs strictly before the event — saying it afterward makes no sense; once results are out, switch to 축하해요 (congrats) or 아쉽네요 (too bad).

mistakes: Saying 행운을 빌어요 after the event is over
It hopes for a future outcome, so it only fits beforehand. After the fact use 축하해요 (good news) or 수고했어요/아쉽네요.
Dropping the particle: 행운 빌어요
The set phrase keeps the object marker — 행운을 빌어요. Omitting 을 sounds clipped and incomplete.
Confusing prayer-빌다 with borrow-빌리다
행운을 빌어요 uses 빌다 (to pray/wish). 빌리다 means to borrow and is unrelated; don't blend them.

usage: raises the listener — for elders, bosses, formal joy
warm and equal, to a peer or friend
생신 is the honorific of 생일
examples: 합격 축하해! 한턱 쏴.
Congrats on passing! Treat me.
반말 ribbing a friend
결혼 축하드려요. 두 분 행복하세요.
Congratulations on your wedding. Be happy, you two.
everyday — at a wedding, raised with 두 분
승진 축하드립니다, 부장님. 정말 잘되셨어요.
Congratulations on your promotion, sir. I'm so glad.
real situation — to a superior, fully formal -ㅂ니다 + 부장님
nuance: 축하 is Sino-Korean 祝賀 ('celebrate-congratulate'), and the form splits by humility: 축하해요 uses plain 하다, while 축하드려요 swaps in 드리다 ('to give, humbly'), so you are 'humbly offering' your congratulations and thereby elevating the listener — the natural choice for elders, bosses, in-laws, or weddings. Contrast 축하드려요 vs 축하해요 sharply: same warmth, different altitude — 축하해요 levels with a friend, 축하드려요 looks up. It collocates with 진심으로 (sincerely) and the celebrated event as a bare noun in front: 결혼 축하, 합격 축하, 생일 축하. Remember 생일 → 생신 and 생일 축하 → 생신 축하 when the celebrant is a senior. The English-speaker pitfall is treating 'congratulations' as one flat word and defaulting to casual 축하해 with anyone — to a senior that is jarringly familiar; and note Korean fronts the occasion (합격 축하해요), unlike English 'congrats on passing,' so resist inserting extra particles between the event and 축하.

mistakes: Using casual 축하해 toward a senior or boss
반말 to someone you respect sounds disrespectful on a happy occasion. Use the humble 축하드려요/축하드립니다.
Saying 생일 축하드려요 to an elder
For a senior, 생일 becomes the honorific 생신: 생신 축하드려요. Plain 생일 to an elder is a touch impolite.
Inserting a particle: 합격을 축하해요
Colloquial Korean fronts the event directly — 합격 축하해요. Adding 을/를 here sounds stiff and textbook-like.

english: It is cool. / You look great.
examples: 우와, 그 재킷 멋있어!
Whoa, that jacket's cool!
반말 complimenting a friend's clothes
발표하시는 모습이 정말 멋있었어요.
You looked really impressive presenting.
everyday praise of someone's manner; 모습 = the way they appeared
혼자 세계여행 하셨다니, 정말 멋있으세요.
You traveled the world alone? You're really amazing.
real situation — admiring a person's life choice, honorific 멋있으세요
nuance: 멋있어요 comes from 멋 (style, flair, class) + 있어요 (to have), literally 'to have flair,' so it praises whatever strikes you as stylish, impressive, or admirable — a look, a skill, a brave decision, even a person's whole vibe. Note it is an adjective built on the 있다 pattern, hence the past is 멋있었어요 and the honorific 멋있으세요. Contrast it with 예뻐요 (pretty) and 잘생겼어요 (good-looking): those judge surface appearance, while 멋있어요 admires coolness and impressiveness that can include character and competence, so a confident speech or a noble act can be 멋있다 but not 예쁘다. Casually you'll also hear the clipped 멋지다/멋져요. The big English-speaker pitfall is the near-homophone 맛있어요 ('tasty,' from 맛 = taste): 멋(eo) vs 맛(a) differ by one vowel, and swapping them turns 'you're cool' into 'you're delicious' — keep 멋 for style, 맛 for flavor.

Only the vowel differs — 멋 (style) vs 맛 (taste). Say 멋있어요 to praise coolness; 맛있어요 is strictly for food.
Using 멋있어요 where you mean simply 'pretty'
멋있어요 admires style/impressiveness, not surface prettiness. For looks use 예뻐요 (pretty) or 잘생겼어요 (handsome).
Conjugating it like a 하다 verb, e.g. 멋있해요
It follows the 있다 adjective pattern: present 멋있어요, past 멋있었어요. There's no 하다 in it.

usage: 너무 = 'so/too,' the most common intensifier here
plain 다 exclamation blurted to yourself
examples: 어머, 너무 귀여워!
Oh my, so cute!
반말 blurted on seeing a puppy; 어머 is a soft 'oh'
아기가 웃는 게 정말 귀여워요.
The way the baby smiles is really cute.
everyday — 게 nominalizes 'the way it smiles'
고양이가 발로 세수해요. 진짜 귀엽다.
The cat washes its face with its paw. So cute.
real situation — describing a charming action, plain-form 귀엽다 to yourself
nuance: 귀여워요 reacts to something small, charming, and lovable — babies, pets, plushies, a child's antics. It is a ㅂ-irregular adjective: the stem 귀엽- drops its ㅂ and adds 워 before vowel endings, giving 귀여워요 (not 귀엽어요) and past 귀여웠어요; this is the same pattern as 춥다 → 추워요 and 덥다 → 더워요, so learning it here transfers widely. Contrast 귀엽다 with 예쁘다 (pretty/beautiful): 예쁘다 admires refined beauty (a flower, a dress, an elegant woman), while 귀엽다 admires adorable, often youthful or tiny charm — calling a stately older person 귀엽다 can sound belittling, whereas 예쁘다 or 멋있다 flatters. The English-speaker pitfall is the conjugation, since the literal-looking 귀엽어요 is wrong, plus the status caution: 'cute' in English is harmless, but 귀여워요 aimed at a senior or someone you should respect can read as condescending, so reserve it for children, pets, peers, or sweethearts.

please eat a lot / help yourself
반말 to a friend or family junior

제가 직접 만들었어요. 맛있게 드세요.

usage: how are you getting on these days?
examples: 야, 잘 지내?
Hey, you doing okay?
반말 checking in on a friend
오랜만이에요. 그동안 잘 지냈어요?
Long time no see. Have you been well?

부모님도 다 잘 지내시죠?
Your parents are doing well too, right?
real situation — asking about someone's family, honorific 지내시죠

Tone alone flips it: rising 잘 지내요? is the question, falling 잘 지내요. is the answer. Contrast it with 어떻게 지내요? (how are you getting on?), which is more open-ended and invites detail, whereas 잘 지내요? gently presumes things are fine and just seeks confirmation; also distinguish it from 기분이 어때요? ('how do you feel?'), which probes mood in the instant, not life in general. Because it spans a stretch of time, the past 잘 지냈어요? is common after a long absence. examples: 어? 오랜만이야! 잘 지냈어?
Oh? Long time no see! Have you been well?
반말 running into a friend
우리 거의 일 년 만이에요. 정말 오랜만이에요.
It's been almost a year. It's really been a while.

오랜만에 뵙겠습니다, 선배님.

real situation — greeting a senior, humble 뵙다 + 선배님
nuance: 오랜만이에요 is 오랜만 ('a long while since,' itself from 오래 = long + 만 = the elapsed-interval marker) + 이에요 (to be), so it states 'it's been a long time' and works as a warm greeting the moment you reunite. The little 만 is the engine: it measures how much time has passed (일 년 만에 = after a whole year, 오랜만에 = after a long time), so anchor on it. Contrast 오랜만이에요 (the greeting, a complete sentence with 이에요) against the adverb 오랜만에 ('after a long time'), which modifies an action — 오랜만에 만나요 (we meet after a long time), 오랜만에 영화 봤어요 (I watched a movie for the first time in ages); mixing them up (saying 오랜만에 as a bare greeting) is a classic slip. The English-speaker pitfall is borrowing 'long time no see' loosely for any short gap — in Korean it genuinely implies a real stretch apart (weeks or months), so greeting someone you saw yesterday with 오랜만이에요 sounds sarcastic or strange; for a short absence, just say 안녕하세요.

오랜만에 is an adverb ('after a long time') needing a verb — 오랜만에 만나요. The greeting form is 오랜만이에요.

The correct word is 오랜만 (오래 + ㄴ + 만). Spelling it 오래만 drops the structure that means 'after a long interval.'

usage: 또 + 보다, the shorter casual version
다음에 = next time, implies a real plan
examples: 오늘 진짜 재밌었어. 또 봐!
Today was really fun. See ya!
반말 parting from a friend
조심히 가세요. 다음에 또 만나요.
Get home safe. See you again next time.

좋은 인연이었어요. 기회 되면 또 만나요.
It was a good connection. Let's meet again if we get the chance.
real situation — a warm but open-ended farewell with 기회 되면
nuance: 또 만나요 joins 또 (again) with 만나다 (to meet) in the 요-form, so it means 'let's meet again' — a hopeful goodbye implying you'd like to see the person another time. Crucially 만나다 means to meet up with a person (a scheduled or sought encounter), distinct from 보다 ('to see/look'); the casual goodbye 또 봐요 leans on the lighter 보다, while 또 만나요 sounds a touch more intentional, as if you value the relationship. Note 만나다 takes 을/를 or the comitative 와/과 (친구를 만나요 / 친구와 만나요), not 에서, for the person met. Contrast it with the time-buying 다음에 봐요 (see you next time, vaguer) and with 안녕히 가세요/계세요, the neutral 'goodbye' that carries no promise of reunion — 또 만나요 specifically projects a future meeting. The English-speaker pitfall is reflexively saying 'see you' to someone you'll likely never meet again the way English does; in Korean 또 만나요 sets up a genuine expectation of meeting, so for a one-off encounter with no plan to reconnect, the cleaner farewell is 안녕히 가세요.
